newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen higher at open, cheers Fed.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen higher at open, cheers Fed.

text.p: Wall Street is seen opening higher Wednesday, extending a rally begun after the Federal Reserve decided to leave interest rates unchanged.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged following the Fed news yesterday, closing up 74.58 points at 7303.46 after spending most of the day on negative ground. Bonds also rose.

The Dow roared up on a wave of relief when the Federal Open Market Committee said it would let the key federal funds rate remain at 5.5 percent. Analysts had been split over whether rates would be raised.

"It looks like Wall Street will continue to cheer the Fed's decision not to raise rates this morning," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "This is a positive for stock markets."

Financial and technology shares, which closed sharply higher yesterday, were expected to lead the way higher today, analysts said. Financial stocks have been hurt recently by fears of an interest rate hike.
Among U.S. high-technology stocks, Dell Computer Corp shares bounced in after-market trade as the company reported a sharp rise in first quarter earnings.
"The market will continue to celebrate the Dell quarter and we should see some follow-through from yesterday," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
But analysts cautioned that an ebullient stock market could fall prey to profit-taking later in the day.
Dell posted first quarter earnings of $1.08 per share, up from $0.42 a year ago.

Other technology stocks were expected to be boosted by the Dell results. Yesterday the technology-heavy Nasdaq, firm for most of the day, jumped 22.64 points late in the session to finish at 1,363.88.
Investors will also scrutinize U.S. March trade deficit data. The deficit came in at $8.51 billion, against a forecast of $10.3 billion.
Bonds should dictate share prices for the immediate future, Cardillo said, so stocks could rise if bonds firm.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average fell 490.85 points, or 2.41 percent, to 19,841.98.
In London the FTSE 100 was up 33.0 points at 4640.5.
U.S. stocks were mostly higher in London, with shares of high-technology companies exhibiting strength.
The Standard & Poors futures index was up 2.85 points at 847.40, and the long bond was up 2/32 at a 6.90 percent yield.

The dollar recovered againt the yen in Tokyo after a volatile session. But it was off highs that were registered following suggestions by a Bank of Japan deputy governor that the central bank was considering the timing of a rate rise.
The dollar was trading at 113.65/75 yen in Tokyo and at 1.6871/81 marks in Europe.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said growing signs of large inventories at retailers could hurt department-store stocks.
The New York Times's Marketplace column said Xircom insiders profited by selling high then buying low, but Securities and Exchange Commission rules could force them to give up their returns.
